article.overview: A mass spectrometer is an instrument that sorts charged or ionised particles by their mass-to-charge ratio, so that the chemical identity and relative abundance of gases or particles can be determined. In lunar science the term covers instruments that measure the thin lunar exosphere, gases released from the surface or from a lander's own exhaust, and in some cases volatile material in regolith that has been heated or otherwise released for analysis. Scope: this entry covers general-purpose mass spectrometers whose main function is to identify and quantify atoms or molecules by mass. It includes flown instruments (Apollo 17 LACE, Chandrayaan-1 CHACE on the Moon Impact Probe, LADEE NMS, Chandrayaan-2 CHACE-2, and the MSOLO unit that flew on the PRIME-1 payload) and one planned second MSOLO flight. Out of scope and cross-referenced only: gas chromatograph-mass spectrometers (catalogue 71), secondary ion mass spectrometers (73), volatile-specific mass spectrometers (103), volatile analysers (69, 105, 113), and entries called neutral or ion mass spectrometers (140, 141). Ion and energetic-neutral-atom analysers on Chinese and European landers and rovers are related but are not treated as examples, because the sources reviewed did not establish their mass-resolving performance in enough detail to describe them accurately. No lunar landing-site or location recommendations are made.
article.description: A lunar mass spectrometer usually has four parts: an inlet that admits gas or particles from the environment, an ionisation source that gives the particles an electric charge, a mass analyser that separates the ions by mass-to-charge ratio, and a detector that counts the ions arriving at each mass. The instrument's output is a mass spectrum, a plot of signal strength against mass. Each peak corresponds to a species, and the height of the peak indicates its relative abundance. Lunar mass spectrometers have to contend with an environment very different from a laboratory. The lunar exosphere is so tenuous that particle densities are extremely low, so sensitivity matters greatly. At the same time, gases released from the surface, from the lander's own propulsion, or from the instrument's own materials can contaminate the measurement. The Apollo 17 Lunar Atmospheric Composition Experiment (LACE), the LADEE Neutral Mass Spectrometer (NMS), Chandrayaan-2's CHACE-2 and the MSOLO instrument belong to the same broad design family, but their mass ranges, ionisation methods and mass resolutions differ, so they are not directly interchangeable.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purposes of lunar mass spectrometers are: (1) exosphere composition, measuring which species are present in the thin lunar atmosphere and in what proportions. The sources reviewed describe Apollo 17 LACE as finding argon and helium to be the dominant gases, with most of the helium of solar-wind origin and trace amounts of methane, ammonia and carbon dioxide [7]. Chandrayaan-2's CHACE-2 produced what ISRO describes as the first observations of the global distribution of argon-40 in the lunar exosphere [9][10]. (2) Exosphere variability, studying how the exosphere changes with time and with the Sun or solar wind; ISRO states that CHACE-2's objective includes variation of the exosphere over time [9]. (3) Volatile and resource assessment, measuring low-molecular-weight volatiles, including water-related species, in the lunar environment; NASA states that MSOLO is intended to measure volatiles on the lunar surface and to characterise low-molecular-weight isotope ratios [1][3]. (4) Source and loss studies, using composition and isotope measurements to infer where gases come from and how they are lost; the LACE summaries describe thermal escape as the fastest loss route for hydrogen and helium in the sources reviewed [7].
article.operating_principle: Most mass spectrometers used in lunar science follow the same chain of steps. Sampling: gas enters through an aperture or inlet. In LACE the aperture faced upward to sample gases falling toward the surface [7]. In NMS the instrument has open and closed ion sources and several operating modes, including a ram mode with a closed source [4]. Ionisation: neutral atoms or molecules are converted into ions. The sources reviewed describe CHACE-2 as having an electron-impact ionizer [9]; other ionisation approaches exist and the method used for each instrument should be checked against its own documentation. Mass separation: ions are separated by mass-to-charge ratio. Quadrupole mass filters are used in CHACE-2 and NMS, and MSOLO is described by NASA and its component supplier as a modified commercial quadrupole-based mass spectrometer [3][14]. The LACE instrument is described in secondary summaries as a magnetic-deflection neutral mass spectrometer; this design detail was not confirmed against a primary NASA document in this run. Detection: ions reaching the detector are counted. The CHACE-2 detector assembly, as described by ISRO, consists of a Faraday cup and a channel electron multiplier [9]. A quadrupole filter transmits ions of a chosen mass-to-charge ratio while rejecting others, so the instrument can be operated in scan modes that sweep across a range of masses. NMS was described by its PDS entry as having an adaptive scan mode that lets users select bands of mass values to search for unexpected species [4].
article.scientific_importance: A mass spectrometer can identify the species present in a tenuous environment, which is difficult to achieve with remote sensing alone. Exospheric composition helps scientists understand how the Moon interacts with the solar wind, micrometeoroid impacts and its own surface. Isotope ratios, such as the argon-40 to argon-36 ratio, help reveal sources and loss processes. Volatile measurements also matter for planning any future robotic or human use of lunar resources, although the scientific and commercial claims made about specific resources should be assessed independently of this instrument class. The Apollo LACE measurements were an early in situ composition measurement of the lunar atmosphere. The later Chandrayaan-1, LADEE and Chandrayaan-2 missions extended that work with impacting or orbiting instruments, and the NASA and ISRO sources cited describe these results as contributing to a better understanding of exospheric dynamics [7][9].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a lunar mass spectrometer. Mass range, mass resolution, ionisation method, detector design, mass, dimensions and power vary between instruments and mission configurations. The examples below describe specific flown, operated or planned instruments and should not be generalised to the whole class. Where a value is not supported by a source reviewed for this article, it is recorded as null or not publicly specified. Status categories: flown (operated in space); flown, partial or preliminary (flown with limited or unconfirmed operation); planned (agreement or plan, not flown in the sources reviewed).

examples.name: Apollo 17 Lunar Atmospheric Composition Experiment (LACE)
examples.description: Part of the Apollo 17 Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package (ALSEP) in Taurus-Littrow valley, operated on the lunar surface. Described in the sources reviewed as a miniature mass spectrometer [7]; secondary summaries describe it as a magnetic-deflection neutral mass spectrometer. The aperture faced upward to sample gases coming down toward the surface. Activation is reported as 27 December 1972. It operated for ten lunations, mostly at night, because sunrise heating caused high outgassing [7].

mass_range_amu.status: A pre-flight description in a secondary source gives 1 to 110 atomic mass units. This may not reflect the flight configuration and is not verified against a primary NASA document in this run.

examples.science_reported: Argon and helium dominant; most helium of solar-wind origin; trace methane, ammonia and carbon dioxide; thermal escape the fastest loss route for hydrogen and helium [7].
examples.qualification: Mass, dimensions and power not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.

examples.name: Chandrayaan-1 CHandra's Altitudinal Composition Explorer (CHACE) on the Moon Impact Probe
examples.status: Flown; short-duration descent measurement on an impact probe released from the Chandrayaan-1 orbiter, which impacted the Moon.
examples.description: Quadrupole neutral mass spectrometer developed by the Space Physics Laboratory (SPL), Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre, as described in an SPL-hosted summary [11]. The instrument measured the composition of the sunlit lunar exosphere during descent. Secondary sources give conflicting times for the probe's separation on 14 November 2008; the time was not verified and is not used here.

mass_range_amu.status: As reported in the SPL-hosted summary [11]. The full page could not be fetched in this run, so this value is recorded as reported rather than audited against the full document.

examples.science_reported: ISRO summaries describe direct evidence for water and CO2 dominance in the sunlit lunar exosphere, and heavier constituents above 60 amu [11]. Peer-reviewed follow-up work is listed in the references but was not read in full.
examples.qualification: Mass, dimensions and power not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.

examples.name: LADEE Neutral Mass Spectrometer (NMS)
examples.status: Flown. Operated in lunar orbit on the Lunar Atmosphere and Dust Environment Explorer (LADEE). Launched 6 September 2013 (7 September UTC) from Wallops Flight Facility; mission ended with a planned impact on 18 April 2014 (UTC) [16].
examples.description: Described by its PDS entry as a highly sensitive quadrupole mass spectrometer with unit mass resolution and an adaptive scan mode that lets users select bands of mass values to search for unexpected species [4]. Two ion sources: open source, operated in tilt or survey mode and ion mode; and closed source, operated in ram mode [4]. Science targets: composition and temporal and spatial variability of the lunar exosphere, including species such as helium, argon and radon [4][5] (summary of the PDS description).

mass_range_amu.value: Up to 150 Dalton (per the PDS entry) [4]
mass_range_amu.status: A secondary search summary reports a lower bound of 2 Da from a PDS-hosted document, while another summary gives 1 u. This discrepancy is not resolved against the primary PDS calibration document in this run.

examples.science_reported: Exospheric composition and variability, including helium, argon and radon [4].
examples.qualification: Mass, power, dimensions and data rate were not confirmed against the primary PDS calibration or reference document in this run. Values appearing in secondary summaries were not verified and are left null.
examples.heritage_note: A secondary summary describes NMS as derived from an engineering unit of the CONTOUR NGIMS instrument with modifications for sensitivity and field of view. Not verified against [5] or [6].

examples.name: Chandrayaan-2 CHandra's Atmospheric Composition Explorer-2 (CHACE-2)
examples.status: Flown and operating on the Chandrayaan-2 orbiter. A search summary reports that the orbiter was unaffected by the failure of its lander and carries multiple instruments; this was not verified against the ISRO page in this run [9].
examples.description: Quadrupole mass spectrometer described by ISRO as a quadrupole based neutral mass spectrometer, with a mass range of 1 to 300 atomic mass units and a mass resolution of about 0.5 amu [9]. The detector assembly consists of a Faraday cup and a channel electron multiplier. The sensor probe also includes an electron-impact ionizer and a Bayard-Alpert collector for total-pressure measurement [9]. Heritage: successor to the CHACE instrument on Chandrayaan-1, drawing on the Mars Exospheric Neutral Composition Analyser (MENCA) on India's Mars Orbiter Mission [9].

mass_range_amu.status: As stated on the ISRO page [9].

examples.science_reported: ISRO describes first-of-its-kind observations of the global distribution of argon-40 in the lunar exosphere [9]. The associated paper in Geophysical Research Letters is listed in the references [10]; its full text was not accessible in this run.
examples.qualification: Mass, power and dimensions not stated on the ISRO page. ISRO refers to an instrument payload handbook that was not read in this run.

examples.name: Mass Spectrometer Observing Lunar Operations (MSOLO) on the PRIME-1 payload (Intuitive Machines IM-2 / Athena)
examples.type: Flown lunar surface instrument (2025), partial and preliminary operation
examples.status: Flown, with partial and preliminary operation. MSOLO was the mass spectrometer of the Polar Resources Ice Mining Experiment-1 (PRIME-1), which flew on the Intuitive Machines IM-2 mission using the Nova-C lander under NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services initiative [1][12]. Athena landed near the lunar south pole on 6 March 2025 and tipped onto its side [12].
examples.description: A commercial off-the-shelf mass spectrometer modified to work in space, described by NASA as a commercial off-the-shelf mass spectrometer modified to work in space [1][3]. The main component is a quadrupole mass filter; INFICON, the component supplier, reports a Transpector MPH quadrupole [14]. NASA reports that MSOLO completed testing at Kennedy Space Center, including vibration and a mass-properties test that concluded on 22 November 2022 [1]. NASA states that MSOLO demonstrated the full range of its hardware in lunar conditions during IM-2 [3]. INFICON reports that the instrument ran for several hours until the lander's battery was depleted and produced 136 spectra [14]. A 2026 NASA slide presentation, which could not be read in full in this run, reportedly states that surface sensitivity was lower than in transit, with dust on the instrument suspected, and that some readings may reflect the lander's propulsion exhaust [13].

mass_range_amu.status: Not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.

examples.science_reported: Preliminary. Lander-related contamination is reported to affect gas readings; no peer-reviewed analysis was found.
examples.qualification: Mass, dimensions and power not given in the NASA sources reviewed [1] and not publicly specified in the sources reviewed for this article.

examples.name: Second MSOLO unit on a commercial rover (planned)
examples.status: Planned. Not flown according to the sources reviewed. A reimbursable Cooperative Research and Development Agreement (CRADA) with Magna Petra Corp. was signed on 2 April (2025, inferred from the article date). NASA retains ownership of MSOLO throughout the mission [3].
examples.description: NASA states that the second MSOLO unit will be integrated on a commercial rover selected by Magna Petra and will launch to the Moon no earlier than 2026 [3]. The rover is not named in the NASA article, and no interface, mass or compatibility data for it was verified. Measurement goal: low-molecular-weight volatiles, with the stated aim of inferring the presence of rare isotopes such as helium-3 [3]. The helium-3 resource claim is a commercial aim, not an established measurement result, and it has not been assessed independently here.
examples.qualification: No launch date, launch vehicle, rover identity or interface document was verified.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No universal dimensions exist for a lunar mass spectrometer. Dimensions are not publicly specified for LACE, CHACE (Chandrayaan-1), LADEE NMS, CHACE-2 or MSOLO in the sources reviewed, so they are recorded as null. Instrument form factors differ across the examples, and no proportions are inferred from unlike designs.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Mass is not publicly specified for any example in the sources reviewed. Values appearing in secondary summaries (for example LADEE NMS) were not confirmed against primary PDS documentation and are not used. Mass determines launch and lander allocation, so the flown and planned instruments should be checked against verified mission documentation before any transportation assessment.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Power is not publicly specified for any example in the sources reviewed. Thermal and power requirements are instrument-specific and depend on operating modes, warm-up and heating needs, and the host spacecraft's interface.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A lunar mass spectrometer must operate in ultra-high vacuum, with wide temperature swings between lunar day and night, and exposure to radiation, micrometeoroid impacts and dust. LACE experienced high outgassing after sunrise, which constrained daytime operation and limited measurements to mostly nighttime collection [7]. The MSOLO results show that a lander's own propulsion exhaust, and the instrument's surface condition, can strongly affect measurements [13][14]. Inlet design, timing relative to lander operations and protection of the sampling path are therefore key requirements. NASA's 2026 presentation reportedly identifies dust on the instrument as a possible cause of lower surface sensitivity [13], so dust protection and cleaning options are part of operational planning, although no design details were verified here. A secondary search summary reports that NMS shared orbital measurement time with the LDEX and UVS instruments; this was not confirmed against the PDS pages in this run. Power and data figures for NMS, MSOLO and CHACE-2 were not verified against a primary source in this run.
article.limitations: A mass spectrometer identifies particles by mass but cannot always determine their source; exospheric and lander-related gases can have similar masses and may be hard to separate. Mass resolution limits how well neighbouring species can be separated. LADEE NMS is described as unit-mass resolution [4], whereas CHACE-2 is described as having about 0.5 amu resolution [9]. The sampled environment may be contaminated by the lander or by the instrument itself, as the MSOLO results illustrate [13][14]. Sensitivity can degrade with surface conditions such as dust, and a result recorded at one time may not represent another. Mass range, mass resolution, ionisation method and detector design differ across the examples, so values should not be compared directly without checking each instrument's own documentation. Several values recorded in secondary summaries were not confirmed against primary documents and are therefore not used as established specifications.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: Mass spectrometers in this entry have flown as part of an Apollo surface experiments package, as an impact-probe payload, as an orbiter payload, and as a lander payload. The planned second MSOLO unit is to fly on a commercial rover.
transportation_process: Integrate the instrument into a spacecraft, lander or rover payload compartment or mounting on Earth.
Launch it on a launch vehicle (for LADEE NMS, a Minotaur V from Wallops Flight Facility on 6 September 2013, 7 September UTC [16]).
Transfer to the Moon, or to lunar orbit, using the host vehicle's propulsion.
Deliver to the surface by lander, or install on a probe or orbiter that is commissioned in lunar orbit or on a descent trajectory.
Position the inlet or aperture for sampling, protect the sampling path, and connect power, data and thermal interfaces to the host.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Apollo 17 LACE was deployed by astronauts as part of the ALSEP package, with its aperture oriented upward to sample gases falling toward the surface [7]. MSOLO was carried as part of the PRIME-1 payload on the IM-2 mission using the Nova-C lander [1][12]. The planned second MSOLO unit is to fly on a commercial rover; the rover's transport, mobility and integration arrangements were not verified in this run [3]. CHACE on Chandrayaan-1 flew on the Moon Impact Probe, released from the orbiter and impacting the Moon [11]. CHACE-2 is an orbiter payload on Chandrayaan-2 [9].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: LACE (Apollo 17, 1972), CHACE on the Moon Impact Probe (Chandrayaan-1, 2008), LADEE NMS (2013-2014), CHACE-2 (Chandrayaan-2, operating) and MSOLO on PRIME-1 (IM-2, 2025, partial operation).
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility claims are made for any named lander, rover or spacecraft beyond the flights documented above. A future lunar mass spectrometer's compatibility with a specific vehicle would need to be assessed against verified mass, dimensions, power, thermal, data and inlet requirements and against the vehicle's verified interface documents. No such verification was performed for this article. The NMS PDS description identifies an RS-422 high-speed serial interface, but this detail came from a secondary search summary and was not confirmed against the PDS document in this run [5].

article.historical_significance: Apollo 17 LACE (1972) was a follow-on to the Cold Cathode Gauge experiments flown on Apollo 14 and Apollo 15, which had shown that a tenuous atmosphere existed but could not identify its composition [7]. LACE provided an early in situ measurement of the lunar atmosphere's composition. Chandrayaan-1 CHACE (2008) extended the in situ approach to a probe descending through the sunlit lunar exosphere [11]. LADEE NMS (2013-2014) was one of the instruments on the LADEE mission, which studied the lunar exosphere and dust environment from orbit [4][16]. Chandrayaan-2 CHACE-2 reports the first global observations of argon-40 in the lunar exosphere and extends the Chandrayaan-1 heritage to an orbiter [9][10]. MSOLO (2025) was flown under NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services framework on the PRIME-1 payload; its flight results are preliminary and were affected by lander-related contamination, so its scientific value remains to be established [3][13][14].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: Primary documents not read: the LADEE NMS calibration and reference documents, the Apollo 17 Preliminary Science Report, the CHACE-2 Geophysical Research Letters paper, the Mahaffy et al. (2014) NMS paper and the NASA PRIME-1 MSOLO slides could not be read in full in this run; statements relying on them are attributed to secondary or search-summary sources and should be verified before use. Missing mass and power values: mass, dimensions and power for LACE, CHACE (Chandrayaan-1), NMS, CHACE-2 and MSOLO are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed and are recorded as null. Mass range discrepancies: sources give different lower bounds for NMS (1 u and 2 Da); the LACE pre-flight range of 1 to 110 amu is from a secondary source and may not reflect flight configuration. MSOLO outcome: reported results are preliminary and derived from a vendor article and a NASA slide presentation that could not be read in full; no peer-reviewed analysis was found. Planned MSOLO flight: the second unit is a planned flight only; no launch date, rover identity or interface document was verified. Helium-3 and resource claims: the commercial goal of finding helium-3 is an aim stated by a partner company and NASA, is not evidence of a resource, and is not assessed here. Photograph licensing: the LACE photograph is referenced from a press image page without a verified direct asset URL, and its photographer and usage rights should be confirmed from NASA's archive before reuse.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery. Where no direct asset URL was verified, image_url is null and the source page is referenced instead.

data_quality_notes: Primary documents not read in full: the LADEE NMS calibration and SIS documents (binary PDFs; WebFetch returned only raw bytes and no local PDF renderer is installed), the Apollo 17 Preliminary Science Report, the CHACE-2 Geophysical Research Letters paper (publisher returned HTTP 403), the Mahaffy et al. 2014 NMS paper, and the 2026 NASA MSOLO PRIME-1 slides (binary PDF). Statements relying on them are attributed to secondary or search-summary sources.

Mass, dimensions and power are null for all instruments. Secondary summaries reported values for LADEE NMS (mass, power, dimensions, data rate) and for MSOLO, but these were not confirmed against primary documents and were deliberately not recorded.

LADEE NMS mass range discrepancy: the PDS instrument page gives 'to 150 Dalton'; a secondary summary reports a lower bound of 2 Da from a PDS document and another reports 1 u. Not resolved against the primary PDS calibration document.

LACE mass range: the only value found (1 to 110 amu) is from a pre-flight description in a secondary source and may not reflect flight configuration. LACE mass, dimensions, power and the magnetic-deflection design detail are not confirmed against a primary NASA document.

CHACE on Chandrayaan-1 (Moon Impact Probe) mass range 1 to 100 amu was taken from an SPL-hosted summary surfaced by search; the SPL page could not be fetched in full in this run. Secondary sources also disagree on the probe separation time on 14 November 2008; the time is not used.

MSOLO outcome: results are preliminary. The NASA 2026 slide presentation could not be read in full; its statements (surface sensitivity lower than in transit, dust suspected, possible lander-exhaust contribution) are taken from a search summary. The 136-spectra figure is from a vendor article. No peer-reviewed analysis was found.

The second MSOLO unit on a commercial rover is planned only. The rover is not named in the NASA article; no launch date, launch vehicle, rover interface, or compatibility data was verified. The CRADA signing year (2025) is inferred from the article date.

MSOLO image (msolo.jpg): HTTP 200 and image/jpeg content type were verified, and the file is linked from NASA's image-detail page. Its visual content was not independently inspected in this run, and NASA does not list a credit. The direct-asset verification boolean is therefore recorded as false.

LACE photograph: no official direct asset URL was verified. The EurekAlert press page's low-resolution rendition is a proxy-style media endpoint and was not used. The caption attributes the photograph to astronaut Harrison Schmitt; a catalogued NASA archive number (S72-37255) reported by a secondary site was not verified. Rights should be confirmed from NASA's Apollo image archive.

The Chandrayaan-2 orbiter status (operating; unaffected by lander failure) is from a search summary, and the ISRO page does not give mass, power or dimensions for CHACE-2. An instrument payload handbook referenced by ISRO was not read.

Dates for LADEE (launch 6 September 2013, 7 September UTC; end 18 April 2014 UTC) are from search summaries of NASA pages, and sources differ by one day for the end date. The LADEE end date and the 'planned impact' wording should be confirmed from the NASA mission page in full.

Cross-reference scope: ion and energetic-neutral-atom analysers on Chinese and European landers and rovers (for example, instruments referenced in search results for Chang'e-4, Chang'e-6 and Chang'e-7) are related but are not described as examples here, because their mass-resolving performance was not verified. They should be considered under catalogue entries 140 and 141 when those are written.
Helium-3 resource statements in the MSOLO CRADA material are a partner company's and NASA's stated aims. They are recorded as aims and not as evidence of a resource.
